reasoning: A release-level test plan and feature-level test cases or scripts are different deliverables, written at different times, at different levels and reviewed separately, so this is a different kind of item rather than alternative forms of one output. X's work item ('a test plan or test case set') mixes two levels of handover. Y separates them cleanly.

Monitoring bug resolution is ongoing and should be recast into the items it produces, as in Example B. X's 'status update' is a keystroke-level step with no clear handover. Y names the real units: a fixed defect verified and closed or reopened, and a periodic defect-status report that tracks successes.

QA input to design reviews is commonly given both live in review meetings and as written comments on circulated design or requirements documents. The written comments are a deliverable the design owner relies on. Y reflects this two-place pattern, while X drops the checkable written part.

Standards, methods and procedures for judging quality or release readiness are usually written together as one criteria or quality document. Splitting them, as Y does, is artificial and invents a boundary the workplace does not use. X follows the 'alternative forms of the same deliverable' rule.

Installing and maintaining a testing tool are the same kind of tool-administration change (install, configure, upgrade), handled one ticket at a time. Using the tool to run tests is a different activity. Y's two-part split captures this without X's thin three-way division.

Testers give usability and functionality feedback both as written notes or tickets on a build and in live conversations with developers (standups, desk-side, triage). The spoken part produces nothing checkable. X's split by where the feedback is given follows the instructions, while Y treats all feedback as a written deliverable.

Continuous monitoring should be recast into its items, as in Example B. In practice QA performance monitoring yields both individual anomalies investigated and per-release or periodic performance reports. Y captures both, and X drops the reporting output.

Coordinating user acceptance or third-party testing in practice involves setting up the round, live check-ins and issue triage with participants during testing, and consolidating results for sign-off. These are different activities with different outputs. Y's single item stops at distributing information, so it leaves out a large share of the work.

Y codes the visit as one evaluation whose documented findings the product team relies on, which matches how such visits are handed over.
